en: The *Liaoben Shengsi Jing* (Sūtra on Understanding Birth and Death), translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian.
The Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu sees dependent origination, he sees the Dharma; having seen the Dharma, he sees [the Tathāgata]."
"I. Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable friends!"
The Buddha said:
"If bhikṣus see dependent origination, they see the Dharma; having seen the Dharma, they see the self.
What is the meaning of this?
This is called seeing with conditions.
To see dependent origination as being neither a life-principle nor not a life-principle is to see the Dharma;
to see the Dharma as being neither a life-principle nor not a life-principle is to see the Buddha.
One should follow this wisdom.
"There are two factors by which one perceives external dependent origination, and two factors by which one perceives internal dependent origination; together these constitute four.
What are the two factors by which one perceives external dependent origination?"
It is bound by the characteristics of causes and bound by the characteristics of conditions. What are the characteristics of causes?
From seeds come roots; from roots come leaves; from leaves come stems; from stems come nodes; from nodes come buds; and from flowers come fruits.
This is what is meant by bondage through causal signs (*hetu-nimitta-bandhana*). What is meant by bondage through conditional signs (*pratyaya-nimitta-bandhana*)?
It refers to the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, and space element; from these causes and conditions, the various seeds arise therein.
The earth serves as the support for the seed; water moistens the seed; fire provides heat to the seed; wind causes the seed to sprout; and space allows the seed to be unimpeded.
When these conditions meet with the proper season, they cause the seed to grow.
The seed does not know that it gives rise to the root, nor does the root know that it exists because of the seed;
the root does not know that it gives rise to the leaf, nor does the leaf know that it exists because of the root;

the leaf does not know that it gives rise to the stem, nor does the stem know that it exists because of the leaf; and even the nodes, buds, flowers, and fruits do not themselves know how they arise through this successive production.
Furthermore, the earth does not know that it gives birth to the seed, nor does the seed know that it is sustained by the earth;
water does not know that it moistens the seed, nor does the seed know that it is moistened by the water;
this extends to fire, wind, and space, none of which know one another.
These worthy ones arise from causes and conditions; when the time and assembly are met, they cause the seeds to sprout.
This is not created by oneself, nor created by another, nor does it arise without a cause.
One should perceive external dependent origination through five aspects.
What are these five? First, impermanence;
second, non-interruption; third, non-transmigration; fourth, the non-perishing of the seeds; and fifth, the non-identity of characteristics.

That the seed has already perished is "impermanence"; that the root emerges from it is "non-interruption"; that the seed and the root are distinct is "not remaining stationary"; that many fruits are produced from a small seed is "non-destruction"; and that the production of fruit is like the seed and root, yet not the seed itself, is "the characteristic of non-identity."
"You should know that these two matters are seen as internal dependent origination:
bondage by way of causes and bondage by way of conditions.
What is meant by 'bondage by way of causes'?"
With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises.
Conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise;
conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises;
conditioned by contact, feeling arises.
Conditioned by feeling is craving;
conditioned by craving is clinging;
conditioned by clinging is existence.
Conditioned by existence is birth;
conditioned by birth come old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and mental distress.
Thus, this entire mass of suffering comes into being.
That ignorance does not know that it produces volitional formations, nor do the volitional formations know that they arise from ignorance;
the volitional formations do not know that they produce consciousness, nor does consciousness know that it arises from the volitional formations;
consciousness does not know that it produces name-and-form, nor does name-and-form know that it arises from consciousness.
The six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and even aging and death likewise revolve without being known.

From this lack of clear understanding (*avidyā*) there is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); from volitional formations there is consciousness (*vijñāna*); from consciousness there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); from name-and-form there are the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and mental distress, as explained above.
This is merely the nature of great suffering that exists as a complete whole.
If there were no birth, then there would be no aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, or mental distress.
"Venerable ones, because of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there are phenomena that arise conditioned by it;

there are phenomena that arise conditioned by it but are not dependent origination itself; there are phenomena that are dependent origination but do not arise conditioned by it; and there are phenomena that are neither dependent origination nor arising conditioned by it."
"What is meant by 'dharmas that arise through conditions but do not arise without conditions'? It is:
with ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations;
with volitional formations as condition, there is consciousness."
With consciousness as condition, there are name-and-form, and so on, up to old age and death; thus the great mass of suffering comes to be, as explained above.
This is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), not dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*).
"What is meant by 'dharmas produced by conditions' that are not 'dependently originated'?
It refers to ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age and death."
This is called "dependently arisen phenomena" (pratītyasamutpanna-dharma), not "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda). What is meant by "dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena"?

It refers to that which arises, abides, and does not cease from the production of old age and death. This arising is proximate through its cause, proximate through its condition, proximate through its subtle cause, proximate through its truth, proximate through its suchness, proximate without difference, proximate without delusion, and proximate as dependent origination; it is by means of these conditions that such phenomena are produced.
Existence, feeling, craving, sensation, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and formations—
these are called phenomena that arise through conditions and are dependently originated.
What are phenomena that do not arise through conditions and are not dependently originated?
This refers to one who has attained the Path.
What is meant by "lack of clarity"?
It is as follows, in six ways.
The six kinds of sensation belong to either women or men.
What are these six?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
That the body remains stable is the earth element;
that it is maintained without dispersal is the water element;
that food, drink, taste, and mastication are well digested through rest is the fire element.
The exhalation and inhalation within the body constitute the element of wind;
that which cannot be sustained by the four great elements constitutes the element of space;
and their movement like the pulling of a double bowstring constitutes the element of consciousness.

Just as that element of earth is neither female nor male, neither a person nor a man, neither the body nor the locus of the body, neither born of a human nor a youth, neither an agent nor a non-agent, neither one who abides nor a non-abider, neither wisdom nor a non-wise one, neither a sentient being nor a self, nor "mine," it has no owner and is not possessed by anyone.
The elements of water, fire, wind, and space are likewise.

The element of consciousness is neither female, nor male, nor human, nor person; it is not the body, nor that which belongs to the body; it is not born of a person, nor is it a youth; it is neither an agent nor one who lacks agency; it is neither abiding nor one who abides; it is neither wisdom nor one who lacks wisdom; it is not a sentient being, nor "mine," nor "I," nor does it possess anything, nor does it have a master.

Thus, based solely on these six kinds of perceptions—perception of unity, perception of combination, perception of woman, perception of man, perception of delusion, perception of self, perception of mastery, and perception of sovereign power—one undergoes various types of experience; therefore, this is called ignorance.
At that time, it was said: "By nature one is deluded, possessing perceptions of purity, permanence, pleasure, and self; these are doubts, resentments, and delusions, not the supreme path.
The Buddha says this is ignorance (*avidyā*), which is also to be defiled by external objects; because wisdom is absent, delusion arises, and thus it is called ignorance.
Because of delusion, there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)."
Because of the cognition of objects, there is consciousness;
because of the five natures, there is name-and-form;
because of dependence on the faculties of name-and-form, there are the six sense bases.
The conjunction of these three constitutes contact (*sparśa*);
from the activity of contact arises sensation (*vedanā*);
and because one delights in sensation, there arises craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Because craving expands further, it constitutes "feeling" (vedanā);
because feeling will again give rise to formations (saṃskāra), it constitutes "existence" (bhava);
because the five natures are fully accomplished, it constitutes "birth" (jāti).
The maturation of the various aggregates constitutes old age;
the cessation of the life-faculty constitutes death;
and the burning within constitutes sorrow.
Deceptive speech constitutes sorrow;
the conjunction with the five bodies of sensory consciousness constitutes the five types of suffering;
and the conjunction with the body of mental consciousness constitutes vexation.
The mental preoccupation with exertion is affliction;
because of existence, there arises further existence.
Seeing and knowing it thus, one obstructs what is manifest as this: it is called complete and fulfilled, for the nature of great suffering is fully present.
From this, one undergoes misfortune and decline; because of attachment, one is born again.
Its beginning cannot be seen or known, nor can it be measured.
Furthermore, "darkness" (ming) signifies the meaning of non-illumination.
To bring about formation is the meaning of "volitional formations" (saṅkhāra);
to know is the meaning of "consciousness" (viññāṇa);
and depending upon that, resting upon that, and mutually relying upon that is the meaning of "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
The primary sense is not exclusively the meaning of the six sense bases;
furthermore, it is combined with the meaning of contact (sparśa);
and from this, the meaning of feeling (vedanā) is understood.
Thirsting for and desiring to obtain objects, like fire that knows no satiety, is the meaning of craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
grasping is the meaning of clinging (*upādāna*);
and that which will come to be again is the meaning of existence (*bhava*).
The five elements (pañca-dhātu) are taken to mean "birth" when they ascend;
"aging" when they mature;
and "death" when their functioning declines.
This explanation of the meaning also constitutes the characteristics of the twelvefold dependent origination.
Furthermore, from ignorance (*avidyā*), one engages in meritorious deeds or engages in deeds that are like those of a criminal; this is called "conditioned by ignorance.
Because there are various formations (*saṃskāra*), based on merit and non-merit, consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises; this is called "conditioned by formations, consciousness."
Through consciousness acting as the formative activity (*saṃskāra*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is fully brought into existence; this is called "conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arises.
Through this arising, there is activity, and with activity there is invariably feeling (*vedanā*); this is called "conditioned by name-and-form, contact (*sparśa*) arises.
The meeting of the six sense bases and visual consciousness results in pleasure; this is called "conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises."
As it is with contact (*sparśa*), so it is with the cognition of sensation (*vedanā*); this is called "sensation arises conditioned by contact.
Because one who does not know sensation acts differently, they suddenly seize upon craving (*tṛṣṇā*) like an elephant; this is called "craving arises conditioned by sensation.
From craving, the elephant swallows again; this is called "existence (*bhava*) arises conditioned by craving."
Feeling consists of the three types of formations—of body, speech, and mind; this is called "conditioned by feeling, there is existence.
When there is the exertion of formations, there will again be the completion of the factors for birth; this is called "conditioned by existence, there is birth.
Because the five natures have already been established, there is old age and death.

This is the twelvefold dependent origination, revolving and turning in succession, performing the work of cultivation. Consciousness performs the act of sowing; ignorance performs the act of counteraction.
It is like the earth supporting the seed, water preventing the seed from dispersing, fire ripening the seed, wind causing the seed to sprout, and space allowing the seed to be unobstructed.
It is the same with the performance of agricultural work: craving moistens the formations, yet those formations do not know,
"I am performing agricultural work," nor does craving know [this].
"I am the moisture for the formations.
Consciousness does not know:
"I am the seed for the formations."
He is neither clear nor aware:
"I am practicing in opposition.
It is just as the earth is unaware:
"I am the one who holds the seed.
Water, fire, wind, and space are as explained above.
From the toil of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*), there shall again be the completion of birth through the possession of the necessary conditions.
Furthermore, there is no one here who steps forth from this world; it is merely the mutual support of causes and conditions.
For example, when a mirror is clean and bright, the image of a face arises in dependence upon internal and external factors.
The face does not die here to be born there; it exists within the mirror, and its causal conditions remain unimpaired.
This is not a case of dying here to be born there, yet there is the experience of suffering; because the causal conditions are unimpaired, from this arises feeling.
Just as fire, through its sensation, manifests continuously day and night yet its flames do not walk, so too is consciousness:
it is not bound by the characteristics of the body as it wanders through the five realms of existence.
Because there are conditions, it arises; this dharma has no master.

It is like the full moon, forty-nine *yojanas* in diameter, whose circular form appears in the water below; though the conditions remain unimpaired, it is not that the moon dies there and is born here.
One should contemplate birth and death in this manner.
This is called bondage through causal characteristics (*hetu-nimitta-bandhana*). What is called bondage through conditional characteristics (*pratyaya-nimitta-bandhana*)?
As the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and forms.
That eye does not know:"
"I practice tranquility.
Form does not know:
"I am the counterpart to consciousness."
Luminosity does not know:
"I am that which illumines consciousness.
Space does not know:
"I shall cause consciousness to be unimpeded.
Consciousness does not know:
"I have produced this existence through volitional formations."
The eye, visible forms, light, space, and attention cause visual consciousness to be fully produced.
Likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, in dependence upon mental objects, give rise to mental consciousness.
The eye does not know:
"I provide a basis for consciousness.
Nor do phenomena know: [the same].
"I am performing the activity for consciousness," the mind does not know;
"I am providing illumination for consciousness."
Space does not know:
"I cause consciousness to be unimpeded.
Consciousness does not know:
"I have accomplished this through these causes and conditions. It is thus, Ānanda!

By depending on the mind, phenomena, clarity, emptiness, and mindfulness, consciousness is fully brought into being. Yet this is not made by itself, nor made by another, nor made by both; it does not arise without a cause. It exists neither because of a self, nor because of another, nor without a cause.
"One should perceive internal dependent origination through five aspects.
What are these five? They are:
it is impermanent, it is not discontinuous, it is not transferred, it is a small action with a great result, and its characteristics are not identical to the original."
That [self] is like the limit of death, for the body has already perished and become non-existent;
yet it arises as a constituent of existence, being uninterrupted.
Whether it goes as the same or goes as something different, because its parts are distinct, it does not walk.
"Little practice with great reward" means that one's practice does not perish.
Just as the retribution of practice arises, it is not from a former household.
If one perceives this dependent origination as being without a life-principle and not a life-principle, this constitutes seeing the Dharma.
To see that phenomena have neither a self nor a life-principle is to perceive the Four Noble Truths:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
It is like a person of clear vision who, seeing a master’s painting, exclaims how excellent the work is and how marvelous the artist’s skill.

It is the same for one who sees the Four Truths: the Buddha knows all and manifests all; from this, one attains joy and does not depart from the Buddha; one attains the Dharma and the Sangha, reaching the state of the Truly Real, and attains joy in the precepts without departing from them.
The Sūtra on Understanding Fundamental Birth and Death (Liaoben shengsi jing)
